method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **LARCs are the contraception of choice for young people.** **Use barrier contraception such as condoms in addition** to reduce STI risk.
claims.source_text: Long-acting reversible contraceptives are the contraception of choice for young people … Barrier contraceptives (eg condoms) should be used in addition to more reliable forms of contraception to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discussing contraception does not increase the likelihood of sexual activity.** Adolescents are the group least likely to use the most reliable methods.
claims.source_text: Discussing contraception does not increase the likelihood of sexual activity … Adolescents are the age group least likely to use the most reliable forms of contraception
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Assess and document whether the adolescent is a mature minor with capacity to consent.** Confidentiality holds unless they are not a mature minor and/or there is significant risk (harm to self or others, physical or sexual abuse).
claims.source_text: Assess and document whether the adolescent fulfills the criteria of a ‘mature minor’ and has capacity to consent to treatment … Adolescents have a legal right to confidential health care unless they cannot be considered a mature minor and/or there is significant concern regarding risk (ie harm to self or others, physical or sexual abuse)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Screen for contraindications:** thromboembolism risk, malabsorption, liver disease, and interacting medicines such as enzyme-inducing anti-epileptics.
claims.source_text: Assess for contraindications to specific contraceptive options. These may include: Risk of thromboembolism Malabsorption Liver disease Medications that may interact with hormonal contraception eg enzyme inducing anti-epileptic medication
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine blood pressure and BMI.** Baseline investigations are not usually needed; **consider an STI screen if sexually active and not screened in the last 12 months.**
claims.source_text: Examination Blood pressure Body mass index (BMI) … Baseline investigations are not usually required … STI screen if sexually active and not performed in the preceding 12 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Explain correct use, side effects and time to efficacy, with written information.** **Review at least 3 months after starting** for adherence, side effects and satisfaction.
claims.source_text: Discuss correct use, anticipated side effects and time to efficacy, provide written patient information … Arrange review at least 3 months post commencement of contraception to assess adherence, side effects and satisfaction with chosen method
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **LARC is most reliable: fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women per year with typical use.**
claims.source_text: Most reliable: Less than 1 pregnancy per 100 women per year with typical use
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Etonogestrel implant (Implanon):** inner upper arm, inserted and removed under local anaesthetic, **effective for up to 3 years**. 20% become amenorrhoeic but 20% have frequent or prolonged bleeding, usually settling within 3 months. ⚠️ **Some enzyme-inducing drugs reduce its efficacy.**
claims.source_text: Etonogestrel implant (Implanon™) Subdermal implant inserted into inner, upper arm Releases progestogen Prevents ovulation, thickens cervical mucus Insertion and removal with local anaesthetic Effective for up to 3 years Over 99% effective Highly effective Minimal user involvement Cost-effective 20% of users become amenorrheic 1 in 3 have lighter and less painful periods Acne may improve Rapid return to normal periods post-removal 20% have frequent or prolonged bleeding Headaches, acne, tender breasts and mood changes possible Side effects may improve with time, irregular menstrual bleeding usually resolves in 3 months Efficacy reduced by some enzyme inducing drugs
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IUDs (levonorgestrel or copper):** commonly inserted under general anaesthetic in this age group; no drug interactions. ⚠️ **Insertion risks: 1 in 500 uterine perforation, 1 in 300 infection, small risk of expulsion.** ⚠️ **Contraindicated with PID and some STIs.**
claims.source_text: Intrauterine devices (IUD) Levonorgestrel IUD Copper IUD Impair sperm motility, fertilisation and implantation Commonly inserted under general anaesthetic, though possible awake Highly effective Minimal user involvement Cost-effective No drug interactions … 1 in 500 risk of uterine perforation, 1 in 300 risk of infection, small risk of expulsion … Contraindicated in patients with pelvic inflammatory disease and some STIs
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mirena LNG-IUD: effective for up to 5 years**, periods lighter and shorter, 20% amenorrhoeic at 1 year. **Kyleena: up to 5 years**, 12% amenorrhoeic at 1 year, more irregular (usually light) bleeding.
claims.source_text: Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena™) Releases small amount of progestogen, that in addition to the above, thickens cervical mucus Effective for up to 5 years Over 99% effective Periods become lighter and shorter 20% amenorrhoeic at 1 year … Levonorgestrel IUD (Kyleena™) Releases small amount of progestogen, that in addition to the above, thickens cervical mucus Effective for up to 5 years Over 99% effective Periods become lighter and shorter 12% amenorrhoeic at 1 year More likely to have irregular menstrual bleeding compared to Mirena™ or Copper IUD. Bleeding is usually light
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Copper IUD: effective for 5–10 years depending on type**, no hormonal side effects, but periods may be heavier and more painful.
claims.source_text: Copper IUD Releases small amount of copper continuously Effective for 5-10 years depending on type Over 99% effective No hormonal side effects Periods may be heavier and more painful
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Medium reliability: 3–7 pregnancies per 100 women per year with typical use.**
claims.source_text: Medium reliability: 3-7 pregnancies per 100 women per year with typical use
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First-choice pill in Australia:** low-dose, **35 micrograms or less ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel or norethisterone** — the 'gold standard' safety profile with low VTE risk; most are on the PBS.
claims.source_text: A low-dose pill containing ≤35 micrograms ethinyloestradiol (EE), and either levonorgestrel or norethisterone is the recommended first choice in Australia. This combination is considered to have the ‘gold standard’ safety profile, with a low risk of VTE. Most low-dose pills are listed on the PBS
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **COC is not reliable if a dose is missed or taken more than 24 hours late**; vomiting, severe diarrhoea, some medicines and malabsorption reduce efficacy. **Contraindicated in malabsorption and severe liver disease.**
claims.source_text: Combined oral contraceptive pill (“the pill”) Daily tablet containing oestrogen and progestogen Prevents ovulation, thickens cervical mucus With typical use, 93% effective. If used perfectly, up to 99% effective Periods usually lighter, less painful, more regular No period if hormone free tablets are skipped Acne can improve Reduction in risk of endometrial cancer Not reliable contraception if dose missed or taken >24 hrs late Vomiting, severe diarrhoea, certain medications or malabsorption reduce efficacy Use is contraindicated in malabsorption and severe liver disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Thrombosis risk factors favour another method:** smoking, raised BMI, immobilisation, personal or family history of thromboembolism or thrombogenic mutations, **migraine with aura**, diabetes with vascular complications, uncontrolled hypertension.
claims.source_text: Risk factors for venous or arterial thrombosis include smoking, increased BMI, immobilisation, personal or family history of thromboembolism or thrombogenic mutations, migraine with aura, diabetes with vascular complications or uncontrolled hypertension. In patients with these conditions, alternative contraception methods are preferrable
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vaginal ring (NuvaRing):** in for 3 weeks every month; may be less effective if removed and not reinserted within 24 hours.
claims.source_text: Combined contraceptive ring (Nuvaring™ Soft plastic ring containing oestrogen and progestogen, inserted into vagina for 3 weeks every month … May be less effective if ring is removed and not reinserted within 24 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Progestogen-only pill — an option if oestrogen is contraindicated or not tolerated.** ⚠️ **Not reliable if taken 3 or more hours late (levonorgestrel/norethisterone POPs) or 24 or more hours late (drospirenone POP).**
claims.source_text: Progestogen only pill (POP) Daily tablet Thickens cervical mucus, may inhibit ovulation With typical use, 93% effective. If used perfectly, up to 99% effective Contraceptive option if oestrogen is contraindicated or not tolerated … Not reliable contraception if dose missed or taken ≥3 hours late (levonorgesterel/ northisterone POPs) or ≥24 hours late (drospirenone POP)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Depot injection every 12 weeks:** 96% effective with typical use; ⚠️ **small decrease in bone density, usually recovering after stopping**; weight gain; periods may take 6–12 months to return.
claims.source_text: Contraceptive injections (“depo”) Injection of progestogen, administered every 12 weeks … With typical use, 96% effective … Weight gain Small decrease in bone density, usually returns to normal after cessation … Return of periods may be delayed up to 6-12 months after cessation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Condoms are not reliable contraception but are effective at reducing STI risk** (88% effective with typical use).
claims.source_text: Condoms are not reliable for contraception, however effective at reducing the risk of STIs … With typical use, 88% effective
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Withdrawal and fertility-awareness methods are not recommended in adolescents.**
claims.source_text: Withdrawal, fertility awareness methods Not recommended in adolescents
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consult the paediatric team if a non-consensual relationship or abuse is suspected**; for suspected sexual assault follow local guidelines — **early specialist consultation is vital.**
claims.source_text: You suspect non-consensual relationship or abuse. If sexual assault is suspected, refer to local guidelines. Early consultation with specialist services is vital
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Contraception' (Last updated October 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Contraception/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult adolescent gynaecology** when medical factors affect eligibility or adherence, or menstrual symptoms do not improve on first-line contraception.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with Adolescent Gynaecology when Significant medical factors may impact on contraceptive eligibility or adherence Significant menstrual symptoms are not improved with first line contraception
